prompt: Which assumption of the line-of-centers model does this section say is definitely not true of real molecules?

choices.text: That all colliding particles are spheres
That a collision needs a minimum energy E_0
choices.why: The section keeps the energy requirement. What it rejects is the picture of every particle as a sphere.

choices.text: That glancing collisions supply less energy
choices.why: That is the line-of-centers model's own improvement, and the section keeps it. The faulty assumption is that the particles are spheres.

choices.text: That molecules move with a range of speeds
choices.why: The speed distribution is not in question. The section's objection is that real molecules are not spheres.

explanation: The line-of-centers model assumed that all colliding particles were spheres, which is definitely not the case. The model must therefore be modified to factor in the orientation of non-spherical particles.

prompt: Why did the hard-sphere and line-of-centers models have no need to consider how the colliding particles are oriented?

choices.text: A sphere looks the same from every direction
Every collision in those models was head-on
choices.why: The line-of-centers model includes glancing collisions through the impact parameter b. Orientation didn't matter because spheres have no distinct sides.

choices.text: Those models ignored collision energy
choices.why: Both threshold models compare an energy with E_0. Orientation was left out because the particles were treated as spheres.

choices.text: They used too few particles for orientation to average out
choices.why: The models describe many collisions, but that is not the reason. A sphere can't be turned to present a different face, so orientation never arose.

explanation: Both models treat the particles as spheres, and a sphere presents the same face whichever way it is turned. Once molecules are non-spherical, which part of each one faces the other becomes part of the collision.

prompt: Two non-spherical molecules collide with more than enough energy, but in one of the incorrect orientations shown in Figure 30.3.1. What happens?

choices.text: They do not react
They react, because the energy exceeds E_0
choices.why: Enough energy is necessary but not sufficient for these molecules. Figure 30.3.1 shows incorrect orientations that do not lead to a reaction.

choices.text: They react, but more slowly
choices.why: An incorrectly oriented collision doesn't give a slower reaction; it gives none. Only the correctly oriented collision in the figure reacts.

choices.text: They react only if the impact parameter is zero
choices.why: Even a head-on collision fails if the molecules are wrongly oriented. Orientation is a separate requirement from b.

explanation: Figure 30.3.1 shows molecules colliding with the correct orientation, which leads to reaction, and two of the many incorrect orientations, which do not. For non-spherical molecules, energy alone doesn't guarantee an effective collision.

prompt: Which of these collisions between two non-spherical molecules can lead to reaction, according to the models of this chapter so far?

choices.text: Enough energy, with the correct orientation
Enough energy, with an incorrect orientation
choices.why: Energy alone is not enough for non-spherical molecules. An incorrectly oriented collision does not lead to reaction.

choices.text: Too little energy, with the correct orientation
choices.why: The right orientation can't make up for too little energy; the energy requirement still holds. A collision needs both.

choices.text: Too little energy, but head-on
choices.why: A head-on collision applies all of E_r, but if E_r is below E_0 that still isn't enough. The collision needs enough energy and the right orientation.

explanation: The threshold and line-of-centers models require enough energy, and this section adds that non-spherical molecules must also be properly oriented. Only a collision that meets both conditions leads to reaction.

prompt: After the modifications of Sections 30.1 to 30.3, which pair of conditions must an effective collision of non-spherical molecules meet?

choices.text: Enough energy along the line of centers, and proper orientation
A large enough cross section, and a high temperature
choices.why: These are conditions on the gas, not on a single collision. A collision is effective if it carries enough energy and the molecules are properly oriented.

choices.text: Proper orientation only; energy no longer matters
choices.why: Orientation is added to the energy requirement, not used instead of it. The collision still needs E_loc > E_0.

choices.text: Enough relative kinetic energy only
choices.why: That was the condition of the hard-sphere threshold model. The later sections add that glancing blows and wrong orientations fail.

explanation: Section 30.1 added a minimum energy E_0, Section 30.2 required that the energy along the line of centers, E_loc, exceed E_0, and this section adds proper orientation. Each step makes fewer of the collisions count as effective.

prompt: Because proper orientation of colliding molecules is necessary, what does the section say about the hard-sphere collision model?

choices.text: It overestimates the number of effective collisions
It underestimates the number of effective collisions
choices.why: The hard-sphere model counts wrongly oriented collisions as effective. Counting too many gives an overestimate.

choices.text: It overestimates the total number of collisions
choices.why: Orientation doesn't change how often the molecules collide. It changes how many of those collisions are effective.

choices.text: It gets the number of effective collisions right but the energy wrong
choices.why: Orientation affects which collisions count, not their energy. The hard-sphere model counts too many as effective.

explanation: The hard-sphere model treats every collision of sufficient energy as effective, including those with the wrong orientation. Since those don't react, the model overestimates the number of effective collisions.

prompt: In a reaction between two non-spherical molecules, only 1 in 4 of the collisions with enough energy has an orientation that leads to reaction. The hard-sphere model counts all of them as effective. By what factor does it overestimate the number of effective collisions?
explanation: The model counts 4 collisions for every 1 that actually reacts, so it overestimates the effective collisions by a factor of 4. This is the kind of error the section says leads to an incorrect value of A.

prompt: The hard-sphere model counts 6.0 × 10^30 collisions m^−3 s^−1 with enough energy as effective, but only 5% of these have the correct orientation. How many effective collisions per cubic meter per second are there, in m^−3 s^−1? (Type it in scientific notation, like 2.5e29.)
explanation: Only the correctly oriented collisions react: 0.05 × 6.0 × 10^30 m^−3 s^−1 = 3.0 × 10^29 m^−3 s^−1. The hard-sphere count is 20 times too large, which is why it overestimates the number of effective collisions.

prompt: Which quantity does the section say the hard-sphere model gets wrong because it ignores orientation?

choices.text: The Arrhenius factor A
The minimum energy E_0
choices.why: Orientation decides which collisions count, not how much energy a reaction needs. The section links it to an incorrect value of A.

choices.text: The mean relative speed ⟨v_r⟩
choices.why: Molecules move at the same speeds whatever their shape. The section says the orientation error shows up in A.

choices.text: The order of the reaction
choices.why: The reaction stays bimolecular, rate = k[Q][B]. Overcounting effective collisions gives an incorrect value of A.

explanation: Counting wrongly oriented collisions as effective inflates the factor in front of the exponential. The section calls this one of the factors that leads to an incorrect value of A from the hard-sphere model.

prompt: For a reaction between non-spherical molecules that must collide in a particular orientation, how is the hard-sphere estimate of A likely to compare with the experimental value?

choices.text: Too large
Too small
choices.why: The model counts wrongly oriented collisions as if they reacted. Counting too many effective collisions makes A too large.

choices.text: About right, since orientation averages out
choices.why: Wrong orientations don't cancel right ones; they simply don't react. Leaving them in makes the estimate too large.

choices.text: Too large or too small with equal chance
choices.why: Ignoring orientation errs in one direction: it adds collisions that don't react. So the estimate of A is too large.

explanation: The hard-sphere model overestimates the number of effective collisions, since it counts collisions with the wrong orientation. A rate built on too many effective collisions gives too large a value of A.

prompt: How does the section describe the role of orientation in the hard-sphere model's incorrect value of A?

choices.text: It is one of the factors
It is the only factor
choices.why: The section calls it one of the factors. The line-of-centers section had already found other problems with σ_r, and internal energy comes next.

choices.text: It has no effect on A
choices.why: The section says the overcounting of effective collisions leads to an incorrect A. It is one of the factors.

choices.text: It affects E_0 rather than A
choices.why: The section ties orientation to the value of A. It says nothing about orientation changing the minimum energy.

explanation: The section says that the need for proper orientation is one of the factors that lead to an incorrect value of A. It doesn't claim to be the whole story; the next section turns to internal energy.

prompt: Reaction 1 is between two nearly spherical particles; reaction 2 is between two non-spherical molecules that must meet in one particular orientation. For which is the hard-sphere estimate of the effective collisions likely to be closer to the truth?

choices.text: Reaction 1, with the nearly spherical particles
Reaction 2, with the non-spherical molecules
choices.why: The hard-sphere model assumes spheres. For non-spherical molecules it also counts the wrongly oriented collisions, so its error is larger.

choices.text: Both equally, since the model ignores shape
choices.why: Ignoring shape costs nothing for spheres but overcounts for molecules that need a particular orientation. The errors are not equal.

choices.text: Neither, since the model never counts collisions
choices.why: The hard-sphere model is built on counting collisions, through Z_QB. It fits spheres better because their orientation doesn't matter.

explanation: For nearly spherical particles orientation hardly matters, so the hard-sphere picture fits them better. For non-spherical molecules many collisions have the wrong orientation, and the model overestimates the effective collisions.

prompt: Figure 30.3.1 shows one correct orientation and two incorrect ones, which the caption calls "two of the many incorrect orientations." What does this suggest about such collisions?

choices.text: Many orientations fail, so many collisions are ineffective
Most orientations work, so orientation hardly matters
choices.why: The caption calls the incorrect orientations many, so many ways of meeting fail. That is exactly why orientation matters.

choices.text: There are only three possible orientations
choices.why: The figure shows just two of the many incorrect orientations. Molecules can meet in many ways, and only some of them react.

choices.text: The correct orientation is the most likely one
choices.why: Nothing favors the correct orientation; it is one of many ways to meet. That is why many collisions are ineffective.

explanation: Non-spherical molecules can meet in many orientations, and only certain ones lead to reaction. So a large share of collisions can be ineffective, which is why the hard-sphere model overestimates the effective collisions.

prompt: The line-of-centers model already allows for glancing collisions through the impact parameter b. What does this section add that it lacks?

choices.text: The orientation of non-spherical molecules
A minimum energy E_0
choices.why: E_0 was introduced in Section 30.1 and is used by the line-of-centers model. This section adds the orientation of non-spherical molecules.

choices.text: The relative speed of the reactants
choices.why: Relative speed and energy were already in the models through v_r and E_r. The new ingredient is orientation.

choices.text: The collision cross section σ_QB
choices.why: σ_QB goes back to the hard-sphere model. The line-of-centers model lacks only a way to handle orientation, since it treats particles as spheres.

explanation: The impact parameter describes how far off-center two spheres collide, but a sphere has no orientation. This section adds the requirement that non-spherical molecules meet in a proper orientation.

prompt: Two non-spherical molecules collide head-on (b = 0) with E_r > E_0, but in an incorrect orientation. How do the line-of-centers model and this section disagree about it?

choices.text: Line of centers counts it as effective; this section says it doesn't react
Both say it reacts, since E_loc = E_r > E_0
choices.why: The line-of-centers model would say so, but this section adds that a wrongly oriented collision does not lead to reaction.

choices.text: Both say it doesn't react, since b = 0
choices.why: b = 0 is the best case in the line-of-centers model, with E_loc = E_r. That model would count this collision as effective.

choices.text: Line of centers says it doesn't react; this section says it does
choices.why: This swaps the two. The line-of-centers model has E_loc = E_r > E_0, so it counts the collision; the orientation requirement rules it out.

explanation: With b = 0, E_loc = E_r > E_0, so the line-of-centers model counts the collision as effective. Because it treats the molecules as spheres, it misses that the wrong orientation prevents reaction, and so it overestimates the effective collisions.

prompt: For which reactants is the need for a specific orientation likely to matter most?

choices.text: Larger, more complex molecules
Nearly spherical particles
choices.why: A sphere looks the same from every side, so its orientation doesn't matter. The requirement matters for non-spherical, complex molecules.

choices.text: The fastest-moving molecules, whatever their shape
choices.why: Speed affects the energy of a collision, not whether orientation matters. Shape decides that: complex, non-spherical molecules are affected most.

choices.text: Molecules at the lowest concentrations
choices.why: Concentration changes how often molecules collide, not which orientations react. Orientation matters for larger, more complex molecules.

explanation: Orientation matters for non-spherical particles, and Figure 30.2.1's caption notes that larger, more complex molecules often require a specific orientation for an effective collision. Spherical particles have no orientation to get wrong.
